summaries.example: Maya decides that practicing piano before playing games is the better choice. When the time comes, she knows this, but she chooses a game instead. She is not confused about the choices, and nobody forces her. This is the kind of puzzle philosophers call weakness of will.
summaries.summary: Weakness of will is the puzzling situation in which a person freely and intentionally does something while judging that another available action would be better overall. Choosing a less healthy or more expensive option is not enough: those choices may still be best when all reasons are considered. The deeper puzzle is why someone would act against their own overall judgment. Socrates and Hare say this cannot really happen. They argue that a true evaluation of what one ought to do guides action, so a person who chooses differently either did not truly make that judgment or could not resist. Davidson accepts that weakness of will happens. He explains that a person may see that all the reasons together favor one action without reaching a final, unconditional decision that it is the action to perform. Acting against this assessment is possible, but it shows a failure of rational self-direction. Later discussions ask whether weakness of will must be irrational, whether it is instead a failure to keep a previous resolution, and whether the idea should be applied to beliefs, groups, or psychological difficulties.
key_ideas: Choosing the more expensive option or the less healthy dessert is not automatically weakness of will. Those choices may still seem best overall.
Weakness of will seems puzzling because people often expect actions to follow their overall judgments.
Socrates and R. M. Hare argued that genuine weakness of will is impossible: if someone truly thinks an action is best and can do it, they will do it.
Donald Davidson argued that weakness of will is possible, but it is a flawed kind of action because the person acts against their own best assessment.
Later philosophers disagree about whether every weak-willed action is irrational and even about what weakness of will means.
Some accounts focus on giving up a plan or resolution, rather than acting against a judgment made at that moment.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic helps us understand how thinking, wanting, deciding, and acting fit together. It also helps explain why some choices seem more puzzling than ordinary mistakes. Studying weakness of will can make us more careful about judging people: being tempted, being forced, changing one’s mind, and acting irrationally are not necessarily the same thing.

important_terms.definition: Choosing an action even though you think another available action would be better overall.
Your opinion about which choice is best when you consider everything important about it.
A reason or feeling that pushes you toward doing something.
Thinking carefully about reasons before deciding what to do.

questions_to_think_about: Can someone really believe one choice is best and still freely choose another?
Is choosing a treat instead of a healthy snack always weak-willed?
Does giving up a plan count as weakness of will if new information appears?
Could a person’s judgment about what is best be mistaken?

summaries.example: Jordan judges that stopping after one episode is the best choice because an exam is tomorrow. Jordan is free to stop, understands the reasons, and still starts another episode while continuing to think stopping would be better overall. This differs from choosing an unhealthy dessert while judging it tastier overall: the latter may involve a trade-off, not weakness of will.
summaries.summary: The philosophical problem of weakness of will concerns an agent who intentionally and freely chooses one option while judging that another is better overall. The comparison with ordinary trade-offs matters: knowing that one dessert is healthier does not show that choosing another is akratic if the agent judges the latter better all things considered. Hare offers a Socratic, strongly internalist account. Evaluative judgments are action-guiding; therefore, if a person genuinely judges that they ought to do something and can do it, acting otherwise shows that the judgment was not genuinely held or that the person was psychologically unable to resist. Davidson accepts that akrasia occurs while retaining a special connection between evaluation and action. He distinguishes a comprehensive but relational judgment that the relevant reasons favor one option from an unconditional conclusion that it is the thing to do. His principle of continence requires action to follow the latter conclusion. Thus akratic action is possible, intentional, and yet irrational: the agent has a reason for acting but no adequate reason, by their own lights, for choosing that action over the alternative. Later philosophers challenge both parts of this account. Some emphasize desires, moods, or immediate rewards; some argue that an agent’s better judgment may itself be mistaken; and Holton identifies weakness of will with failure to keep a resolution. The debate also extends to epistemic akrasia, in which belief conflicts with one’s assessment of the evidence.
key_ideas: The central contrast is between acting against a judgment about one aspect of a choice and acting against one’s assessment of what is best overall.
Hare develops a strongly internalist argument: evaluative judgments guide conduct, and sincerely accepting a first-person imperative involves acting on it when possible.
Davidson preserves a motivational role for evaluation while distinguishing an overall, relational assessment from an unconditional conclusion about what to do.
On Davidson’s account, akratic action is intentional and possible, but irrational because it violates the principle of continence.
Critics argue that Davidson’s account may not allow cases in which someone has an unconditional judgment that one action is best but intentionally performs another.
Later views debate whether akrasia can be rational, whether weakness of will concerns abandoning resolutions, and whether it can apply to belief as well as action.
summaries.why_it_matters: Weakness of will connects ordinary experiences of temptation with theories of agency, rationality, motivation, and responsibility. It forces us to distinguish being compelled from choosing badly, changing one’s mind from abandoning a resolution, and making a substantively good choice from reasoning well. These distinctions matter when we explain behavior and decide how much criticism or responsibility is appropriate.

important_terms.definition: Intentional action that conflicts with an agent’s judgment about which available option is better overall; it is also called akrasia or incontinent action.
A judgment about which option is superior after considering the relevant reasons together, not merely in one respect.
A judgment that one option is better in light of a particular reason or set of reasons, without automatically settling what should be done.
The view that some evaluative judgments have an internal or necessary connection to motivation and action.
The view that evaluation and motivation are not necessarily connected, so desires or other factors may pull action away from judgment.
Davidson’s rational requirement to perform the action judged best on the basis of all available relevant reasons.
An intention formed partly to protect a future action from a contrary inclination, such as a plan to avoid a temptation later.

questions_to_think_about: Does an all-things-considered judgment necessarily motivate action, or can motivation diverge from evaluation?
Is Davidson’s distinction between a comprehensive assessment and an unconditional conclusion convincing?
If a person’s better judgment overlooks an important reason, can acting against it be rational?
Is abandoning a resolution different from changing one’s mind?
Could someone rationally believe that a proposition is true while also believing that their evidence does not support it?

summaries.example: Ava plans to finish her science project before checking social media. She still thinks finishing first is the better choice, and she is able to put her phone away. Nevertheless, she opens the app and keeps scrolling. This is different from choosing pizza instead of a salad while thinking pizza is better overall because she values taste more than health in that situation.
summaries.summary: Weakness of will is usually described as knowingly and intentionally doing something while believing that another available choice is better overall. The word “overall” is important. A person may choose an expensive vacation because it offers a better experience, or choose a rich dessert because it seems better in that situation. Those are not automatically weak-willed choices. The harder case is someone who really thinks one option is best but freely chooses another. Socrates and R. M. Hare argue that this cannot happen in the fullest sense. Hare says evaluative judgments are meant to guide conduct. If a person genuinely judges that they ought to do something and is able to do it, their action should reveal that judgment. An apparent exception must involve inability, overwhelming emotion, or merely repeating what other people think. Davidson agrees that weakness of will exists but tries to explain why it is possible. He separates judgments about which reasons favor an option from a final, unconditional decision about what to do. A person may see that all the reasons considered together favor one choice without fully committing to that choice. If the person then acts differently, the action is possible and intentional, but still irrational because it fails to follow the best available practical reasoning. Later philosophers question whether this kind of action is always irrational, whether desires can pull away from evaluations, and whether weakness of will is really about abandoning earlier resolutions instead.
key_ideas: A person can know that one option is cheaper or healthier and still reasonably choose another option.
The puzzle begins when someone chooses an option while judging that a different option is better overall.
Socrates and Hare deny that true weakness of will is possible, while Davidson argues that it can happen.
Davidson distinguishes seeing that reasons favor an option from making a final judgment that one must choose it.
Some later philosophers think desires and feelings can overpower judgment; others think the action may sometimes be rational despite conflicting with the person’s judgment.
Another approach defines weakness of will as failing to follow a plan or resolution made earlier.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate explains why some bad choices seem understandable while others seem especially puzzling. It also helps separate temptation, compulsion, changing one’s mind, and poor reasoning. Understanding these differences can lead to more careful thinking about self-control and responsibility.

important_terms.definition: Acting on purpose against what you think is the best choice overall, even though the better choice is available.
Your view of which option is best after weighing all the important reasons.
A reason that supports one choice in a particular way, without deciding the whole question by itself.
A connection between a judgment and motivation; internalists say some judgments naturally or necessarily push us toward action.
The idea that judgments and motivation can come apart; desires, moods, or rewards may influence action independently.
Davidson’s idea that rational people should do what their complete set of relevant reasons supports as best.

questions_to_think_about: What makes acting against an overall judgment different from making an ordinary trade-off?
Could a person honestly say, “I know this is the better choice, but I am doing the other thing”?
Should a mistaken judgment have special authority over what someone does?
When does changing a plan become weakness of will?
Are strong temptation and being forced the same?
